title: A Hanging Flowerpot by the Window
description: Make a simple hanging plant display through cords, knots, loops, and familiar garden objects.
cardDescription: Make a simple hanging plant display through cords, knots, loops, and familiar garden objects.
subtheme: A Hanging Flowerpot by the Window
focus: Cords hold the pot while loops and knots connect the support. No named knot patterns are required.
solvingTip: Try a plant part or short household object first.
words: Support holding the flowerpot above the floor
Thick flexible strand used in the plant support
Tied fastening joining or securing the cords
Curved opening formed by bending a cord
Circular fitting at the top of some plant hangers
Container holding the plant and its soil
Living growth hanging near the window
Small pierced decoration threaded onto a cord
Green plant part extending above the pot
Earth around the hanging plant's roots
Liquid supplied to the plant when needed
Glass opening providing light beside the plant
Suspend the flowerpot above a surface
Looped knot tied as a decoration

answerNotes.HANGER: The hanger carries the pot rather than being part of the plant.
answerNotes.CORD: Several cords can share the weight of a small pot.
answerNotes.KNOT: A knot is made from the cord itself rather than a metal fitting.
answerNotes.LOOP: A loop can provide a place for a support to pass through.
answerNotes.RING: The ring gathers the hanging cords into one support point.

title: A Hooked Rug on Its Frame
description: Identify the materials and small repeated actions used to make a traditional hooked rug.
cardDescription: Identify the materials and small repeated actions used to make a traditional hooked rug.
subtheme: A Hooked Rug on Its Frame
focus: Rug hooking pulls loops through a backing. It differs from latch-hook kits and from weaving, though all can produce patterned textile surfaces.
solvingTip: Separate the backing, the tool, and the loops forming the visible surface.
words: Curved tool pulling loops through a rug's backing
Coarse open cloth traditionally used as a rug backing
Raised bend of fabric or yarn forming a hooked rug's surface
Support holding a rug's backing stretched during work
Raised textile surface made by the rug's loops
Small floor covering made on this craft frame
Animal fiber often used in traditional hooking materials
Narrow length of cloth drawn through a backing
Continuous fiber strand usable for some hooked rugs
Design guiding the arrangement of colored loops
Decorative band around a rug's outer edge
Hue distinguishing one area of the textile design
Foundation fabric into which the loops are pulled
To pull a loop through the foundation cloth

answerNotes.HOOK: The hook draws material through the backing; it is separate from the frame holding the work.
answerNotes.BURLAP: Burlap is one possible backing; rug makers also use other suitable fabrics.
answerNotes.LOOP: Loops create the pile rather than being cut-out shapes laid on top afterward.
answerNotes.FRAME: A frame holds the backing steady but is not part of the finished rug's soft surface.
answerNotes.PILE: Pile names the raised surface rather than the flat backing beneath it.

title: Patterns Stamped into Leather
description: Explore leather decoration through small hand tools, repeated motifs, and the surface receiving them.
cardDescription: Explore leather decoration through small hand tools, repeated motifs, and the surface receiving them.
focus: Stamping presses a design into leather. The clues separate the striking tool from the patterned metal tool and from the material being decorated.
solvingTip: Identify what strikes, what carries the pattern, and what receives the mark.
words: Prepared animal-hide material receiving a stamped design
Shaped tool pressed or struck to leave a decorative impression
Broad-headed striking tool used on many leather stamps
Slanted edge or angled cut used in decorative work
Pointed tool making a small hole through leather
Animal skin before or during preparation as a craft material
Hand-held implement used to shape or mark leather
Repeated decorative shape in a stamped pattern
Outer boundary of the leather piece
Stitched join between pieces of leather
Coloring material applied to a prepared hide
Narrow strip used to join or decorate leather edges
Waist accessory commonly made from decorated leather
Visible impression left by a patterned tool

answerNotes.LEATHER: Leather is processed hide; its surface can be cut, impressed, colored, or stitched in different crafts.
answerNotes.STAMP: The stamp carries the pattern, while a mallet provides the impact.
answerNotes.MALLET: A mallet strikes another tool; its head material can vary with the craft.
answerNotes.BEVEL: A bevel describes an angle or a shaping action rather than a separate layer of leather.
answerNotes.AWL: An awl pierces a hole; it does not remove a broad strip like a cutting blade.

title: A Stained-Glass Window Panel
description: Look at a decorative glass panel through colored pieces, joining strips, and the frame around them.
cardDescription: Look at a decorative glass panel through colored pieces, joining strips, and the frame around them.
focus: Stained-glass work combines cut glass with a supporting joining system. Lead came and copper-foil methods are different ways to assemble a panel.
solvingTip: Use the material, join, or shape described, rather than assuming every metal strip has the same name.
words: Word completing ___ glass, decorative colored window work
Channeled metal strip holding edges in traditional glass panels
Metal alloy used to join parts in a glass-panel framework
Thin copper sheet wrapped around glass edges in one method
Single piece of glass within a window or panel
Transparent or translucent material forming the colored pieces
Traditional soft metal used for channeled joining strips
Outer structure supporting the finished panel
Full design guiding the arrangement of glass pieces
Rounded line in a decorative window design
To divide glass along a prepared line
Hue supplied by a piece of decorative glass
Place where panel framework pieces are connected
Boundary wrapped or fitted into a joining strip

answerNotes.STAINED: Stained glass is a broad craft term; color may be introduced through several glassmaking and decorating processes.
answerNotes.CAME: Lead came holds glass edges in channels; copper foil is a different joining approach.
answerNotes.SOLDER: Solder forms joints; it is different from the colored glass pieces themselves.
answerNotes.FOIL: Copper foil and lead came are distinct construction techniques, even when both use soldered joints.
answerNotes.PANE: A pane is a glass piece, not the entire enclosing window frame.

title: Needlepoint Across a Canvas
description: Explore counted canvas embroidery through mesh, diagonal stitches, and the colored yarn making a design.
cardDescription: Explore counted canvas embroidery through mesh, diagonal stitches, and the colored yarn making a design.
focus: Needlepoint works stitches through an open canvas foundation. Its mesh and stitch vocabulary differ from cross-stitch fabric, even though both crafts can use counted patterns.
solvingTip: Separate the foundation cloth from the strand and the path of one stitch.
words: Embroidery worked through an open canvas foundation
Open foundation fabric used for needlepoint

answerNotes.NEEDLEPOINT: Needlepoint commonly uses stitches on canvas; it is distinct from knitting or weaving a new fabric from scratch.
answerNotes.CANVAS: Canvas provides the regular openings through which the stitches pass.
answerNotes.TENT: Tent stitch covers a small diagonal crossing on canvas; the word has a specialized embroidery meaning here.
answerNotes.MESH: Mesh describes the structure of the canvas rather than the colored design worked on it.
answerNotes.TAPESTRY: A tapestry needle commonly has a blunt tip and a large eye, suitable for passing through existing fabric openings.
